variants.answer: I treat payment and refund forms as high-impact flows, so I test them with keyboard and assistive technology—not just automated checks. On a recent project, I mapped the expected tab order, made every field and control reachable with Tab and operable with Enter or Space, and added a clearly visible focus indicator. I associated labels and error messages with their fields, announced validation errors to screen readers, and preserved entered data after a failed submission. I also checked that payment steps and refund status changes were communicated in text, not color alone. In our final test pass, keyboard users could complete the full payment and refund journeys without a mouse, and our accessibility review found no critical issues in those flows.

I also test with a screen reader and make sure users can tell when a payment succeeds or a refund is pending. I’d include these checks in both manual testing and our accessibility review.
